text.p: Zenith Electronics Corp., which makes television and video products, said Wednesday it is teaming up with affiliates of Oracle Corp. and Netscape Communications Corp. to launch new Internet television products.

Zenith, based in Glenview, Ill., said it planned to offer Internet television products -- set-top boxes and integrated television sets -- with interactive capabilities based on System Software from Network Computer Inc., a unit of Oracle.

Following the news, Zenith's stock was up 87.5 cents at $12 after trading at a high of $12.375 on the New York Stock Exchange. Oracle was off $1 to $43.75 on the Nasdaq market amid weakness in the shares of computer software companies.
"It's favourable news ... and fits in with Zenith's production of set-top (decoder) boxes," one analyst said.

In a separate statement issued at the Winter Consumer Electronics Show here, Zenith also said it planned to collaborate on consumer-based Internet software and services with Navio Communications Inc., the consumer affiliate of Netscape.
The products will allow TV viewers to access the World Wide Web, send and receive multimedia e-mail and participate in a variety of interactive and electronic commerce services.
Zenith said it planned to launch its "NetVision" Internet TV products this year, though the company was not specific.
The company said the set-top boxes and televisions will feature a printer port and smart card slot for home shopping, banking and other transactional services.
Zenith said its agreement with Oracle's Network Computer unit marked a new direction for its Internet televison product strategy.
"Working with Oracle, Zenith is redefining the experience of television and marrying channel surfing and net-surfing in a new exciting way," Peter Willmott, Zenith president, said in a statement.
James Barksdale, president of Netscape and a director of privately held Navio, said the Zenith alliance brings Netscape's Internet browser technology into the television market for the first time.
George Podrasky, an analyst at Duff & Phelps Credit Rating Co. said that while the new NetVision products are "potentially positive, it remains to be seen what the consumer really wants."
Robert Gutenstein, an analyst at Kalb, Voorhis & Co., said, "If the consumer should choose to put Internet on his TV, Zenith will be in a good position."
He said that competing consumer electronics companies have moved in a similar direction.

Gutenstein said the latest alliances appeared to be a replacement for Zenith's original plan announced last spring to produce an Internet-linked television product with Diba Inc. of Menlo Park, Calif.
"That has yet to be delivered," he said.
